title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Food & Pharma | PT (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection of 316L tanks, welds and castings in US food, beverage and pharma plants, low-halogen and fully post-cleaned. Request a PT quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Food, Beverage and Pharmaceutical Plants
html:
Liquid penetrant testing finds cracks, lack of fusion and porosity that are open to the surface of stainless steel welds, castings and machined parts in food, beverage and pharmaceutical plants across the United States. Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians with low-halogen, low-sulfur materials and a documented post-cleaning step, so the equipment goes back into hygienic service clean. Request a PT inspection quote with your drawings and cleaning rules.

Why penetrant is the surface method in a hygienic plant

Most product-contact equipment is austenitic stainless steel, usually 316L, and austenitic stainless is not ferromagnetic. That removes magnetic particle inspection from the list, which is why this industry has a penetrant page and no magnetic particle page. Penetrant works on any non-porous metal: it is drawn into a surface-breaking discontinuity by capillary action, pulled back out by a developer, and read as a colored or fluorescent line against a clean background.

It is also the method that most needs planning in a hygienic setting. Penetrant materials are oils, dyes and solvents. A bioprocessing plant is built so that nothing like that should ever remain on a product-contact surface. The technique is therefore as much about cleaning before and after as it is about the examination itself.

Where penetrant is used on process equipment

  • Manual and repair welds on tanks and vessels. Nozzle-to-shell welds, manway rings, sump and bottom welds, clip and lug attachments, and any weld repair on product-contact shells.
  • Jacket and dimple attachment welds. These carry the heating and cooling medium pressure, and cracks start at weld toes and crevices where thermal cycling concentrates stress.
  • Process piping welds that are not orbital. Field welds at tie-ins, branch connections, and fittings welded by hand are examined visually first and by penetrant where the specification requires it.
  • Cast and machined components. Valve bodies, pump housings, agitator hubs and clamp-ferrule fittings can carry cracks, laps or shrinkage open to the surface. The penetrant testing of castings page explains how as-cast surfaces change the technique.
  • Heat-exchanger tubesheets and shell welds on cooling and heating systems.
  • Rework after grinding or repair. A weld that was ground and re-welded gets a surface examination before it is repassivated.

Orbital tube welds on thin hygienic tube are generally accepted by visual criteria, borescope views and sample coupons under ASME BPE, so penetrant is not usually the first choice there. The dye penetrant weld inspection page sets out the examination steps in detail, and the penetrant testing of stainless steel page covers the alloy and chemistry side across other industries.

Rules that frame the work

ASME BPE sets design, welding, surface finish and inspection expectations for bioprocessing equipment. It is not an NDT method standard, so the penetrant examination itself follows ASME Section V Article 6 or ASTM E165, with ASTM E1417 where the specification calls for a fluorescent process control. The 3-A Sanitary Standards add requirements for dairy and food equipment, including smooth, crevice-free product-contact surfaces. FDA current good manufacturing practice rules, namely 21 CFR Parts 210 and 211 for drugs and Part 117 for human food, require equipment that does not contaminate the product and that is cleaned and maintained on a defined program.

Where the vessel or piping is pressure-rated, the construction code supplies the acceptance criteria: ASME Section VIII for vessels and ASME B31.3 for process piping. We apply the criteria you name; we do not choose them. Written procedures are approved by an ASNT Level III, and technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to SNT-TC-1A.

Penetrant materials for stainless steel

Austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys are sensitive to the chemistry left on them. Article 6 therefore limits the sulfur and halogen content of penetrants, removers and developers used on these alloys, and lot-level certification of those limits is obtained from the manufacturer before the job. Chlorides and fluorides are the concern on austenitic stainless because they can promote pitting and stress corrosion cracking, particularly at heat-affected zones and crevices that run warm in service. We bring the batch certificates to site and attach them to the report.

The standard options are:

  • Solvent-removable visible dye with non-aqueous developer for field work. It is portable, controllable, and easy to clean off with a low-residue remover.
  • Fluorescent systems where the specification calls for higher sensitivity. These need a darkened area and ultraviolet lamps, which is hard in a wet washdown room and easier on a bench or in a closed tank.
  • Water-washable systems are less common here because the water carries contaminants into drains that may be validated.

Post-cleaning and hygienic release

After developer is wiped off, the surface is cleaned with the remover specified in the procedure, followed by the cleaning steps your plant requires: detergent wash, rinse to the required water quality, and drying. Whether a surface needs repassivation after penetrant work and cleaning is a decision for your quality unit and the equipment specification, usually under ASTM A967 or A380 practice. We document what was applied, where, and how it was removed, and we do not declare equipment ready for product contact. That release belongs to your quality unit, which may require swab, rinse or total organic carbon checks.

Chemicals brought into a hygienic zone need approval in advance. We supply safety data sheets with the quote and use only the products named in the approved procedure. Flammable solvents are controlled for ventilation and ignition sources, and tank work follows your confined space permit and OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146.

How the examination is done

  1. Prepare. Weld spatter, scale and heat tint are removed by methods your plant approves, because they can mask or fill flaws. Surfaces are not blasted or peened before testing.
  2. Clean and dry. The test area is cleaned and dried so penetrant can enter flaws. The part is within the standard temperature range of Article 6, or the procedure has been qualified for the temperature on the day.
  3. Apply penetrant and dwell. The dwell time comes from the procedure and the material.
  4. Remove excess. Solvent on a lint-free wipe, not sprayed directly onto the surface in a way that washes out indications.
  5. Apply developer. A thin, even coat of non-aqueous developer; indications bleed out and are read within the time window.
  6. Interpret and record. The Level II technician classifies each indication as relevant or non-relevant and measures what is relevant.
  7. Post-clean as described above.

What penetrant finds and misses here

Penetrant shows cracks, lack of fusion, laps, seams and porosity that are open to the surface. It does not find flaws below the surface, tight cracks that are contaminated or smeared closed, or thickness loss. The thickness side belongs to the ultrasonic testing page for food and pharma. A polished or electropolished surface is a good background but can mask very fine flaws, so the technician examines polished welds with magnification and good white light.

What the report contains

Each report records the equipment tag, drawing and revision, material grade, the weld or area examined, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with manufacturer and lot numbers, the sulfur and halogen certification reference, dwell and developer times, surface and ambient temperatures, the technician and level, indications with sketch, location and size, and accept or reject against the code you name. Post-cleaning method and verification references from your plant are attached. We do not calculate remaining life or approve equipment for service.

What to send for a quote

  • Equipment list with tags and alloy grades.
  • Weld maps or drawings that show which welds need examination.
  • Governing code and acceptance criteria, plus your plant's cleaning requirements.
  • Surface finish and any limits on chemicals in the room.
  • Access, ventilation, permits and gowning rules.
  • Site address and the shutdown or changeover window.

Where we work in the United States

  • Indianapolis for pharmaceutical and animal-health plants in central Indiana.
  • Philadelphia for the biologics and generic-drug corridor of Pennsylvania and New Jersey.
  • Newark for New Jersey drug and flavor-ingredient plants with heavy utility piping.
  • Boston for biotech process suites and stainless skid fabrication in Massachusetts.
  • Chicago for food and beverage plants across the Great Lakes region.
  • Omaha for meat, dairy and grain-ingredient plants on the Missouri River.
  • San Francisco for Bay Area biotech and beverage producers.
  • Memphis for processed-food and cold-chain plants in the mid-South.

Planning realities for hygienic sites

Technicians are mobilized to your site for an agreed scope, and the work is scheduled around production, validation windows and changeover cleaning. Penetrant work is wet and solvent-based, so adjacent product, open containers and packaging are protected or removed first, and the area is ventilated. Entry to processing rooms may need gowning, approval of each chemical, and an escort. Ambient conditions matter too: cold washdown rooms and warm jacketed surfaces fall outside the standard temperature range, so the procedure is qualified for the conditions we expect, or the surface is brought into range before we start. Allergen controls, lockout and hot-work permits follow your site rules.

Weld flaws that show up on hygienic stainless

The flaws that matter to a hygienic plant are the ones that create a crevice or a leak path: lack of fusion at the toe of a nozzle or clip weld, crater cracks at the end of a manual pass, porosity that breaks the surface of a ground weld, and fine cracks beside a repair. Each of these can harbor product and survive cleaning cycles, so a visual pass alone is not always enough. Penetrant gives the examiner a mapped, measurable indication that can be accepted, repaired and re-examined, with the same record each time.

Train your own technicians

Plants that want in-house penetrant capability can use PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training, with the penetrant simulator for practice. Your employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, we do not decide passivation or product-contact release, and we do not offer specialist techniques on this page. Magnetic particle testing is not used on 316L, and for the national method background, see the penetrant testing overview.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing safe to use on pharmaceutical product-contact surfaces?
faq.a: It can be, if the procedure plans for it. Low-halogen, low-sulfur materials are used on stainless, the area is post-cleaned to your plant's requirements, and your quality unit decides whether swab, rinse or repassivation steps are required before the equipment returns to product contact.

faq.q: Why not use magnetic particle inspection on 316L tanks?
faq.a: 316L is austenitic and not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particles do not gather at flaws. Penetrant testing detects surface-breaking flaws on any non-porous metal, which is why it is the surface method for stainless process equipment. Carbon steel supports and receivers can still be tested magnetically.

faq.q: Do you test orbital welds on hygienic tube with penetrant?
faq.a: Usually not as the first choice. ASME BPE accepts orbital tube welds on visual criteria, borescope views and sample coupons. Penetrant is used on manual welds, repairs, nozzles, jacket attachments and cast or machined parts where the specification calls for it or a visual result is in doubt.

faq.q: What penetrant materials do you use on stainless steel?
faq.a: We use penetrants, removers and developers whose sulfur and halogen content is certified for use on austenitic stainless and nickel alloys, as ASME Section V Article 6 requires. Lot certificates are obtained from the manufacturer and referenced in the report, and safety data sheets are supplied before mobilizing.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done inside a tank?
faq.a: Yes, after the tank is drained, cleaned and entered under your confined space permit. Solvent vapor needs ventilation and control of ignition sources, and fluorescent work needs a darkened area with ultraviolet lamps. Visible solvent-removable dye is usually the practical choice inside a closed vessel.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is rejectable?
faq.a: The governing code or specification you name sets the criteria, and your engineer or inspector applies them. Our Level II technician classifies indications as relevant or non-relevant, measures them and records accept or reject against the criteria; an ASNT Level III reviews the report.

faq.q: What happens to the surface after penetrant testing?
faq.a: Developer is wiped off and the surface is cleaned with the specified remover, then through your detergent, rinse and drying steps. Whether the area needs repassivation is your quality unit's decision. We document the materials used and how they were removed.

faq.q: What do you need from us for a PT quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment list with alloy grades, weld maps or drawings, governing code and acceptance criteria, your cleaning and chemical rules, surface finish, access and permit details, the site address and the shutdown or changeover window. Then we return a scope with the procedure and materials.

faq.q: When is penetrant the wrong method for a food or pharma plant?
faq.a: Penetrant does not detect subsurface flaws or wall loss, and it struggles on porous or heavily contaminated surfaces. For thickness or internal weld flaws, ultrasonic testing is the better tool. For small-bore orbital welds the accepted approach is visual and borescope examination.
